hero.name: Adidev Panday
hero.tagline: Aspiring Rocket Scientist. AI builder. Researcher.
hero.intro: I'm a Woodstock School student from Ludhiana, India, headed for aerospace engineering: the place where physics, design, and code meet. I build AI-driven apps, publish research, and spend my spare hours on F1 aerodynamics, the violin, and football. This is everything I've made and earned, in one place.

paragraphs: I grew up in Ludhiana, Punjab, and study at Woodstock School, taking HL Physics, Math AA, and Computer Science in the IB Diploma. My focus is aerospace engineering, where rigorous physics meets real design.

Outside class, I build things. I've shipped AI-powered web apps, developed a React Native app to tackle teen drunk-driving in my hometown, and published research on the risks of digital trading. I co-founded my school's AI Club, lead the yearbook as Editor in Chief, and play first chair violin in the Advanced Orchestra. I've competed in varsity football and basketball, interned in product development and CAD, and served on the Academic Honesty Council.
I'm drawn to problems that reward both rigor and creativity: from modeling 4th-down football decisions with game theory to studying how a paper plane's wing generates lift.

research.title: The Rise of Digital Trading: Accessibility Versus Risk of Financial Ruin
research.journal: International Journal of High School Research (IJHSR), Vol. 8, Issue 12
research.pageNote: Paper begins on page 89 of the issue.
research.abstract: Commission-free apps put the stock market in every teenager's pocket, and the same tap that opens a trade opens a trapdoor. This paper examines the double-edged nature of digital trading platforms, weighing the access they hand ordinary investors against the risk of financial ruin that access invites. Drawing on data across major platforms, it follows three threads, accessibility, behavioral effects, and financial competence, and asks what frictionless trading really costs the people it claims to set free.

extracurriculars.description: Five years ago I picked up a violin with zero musical background and sat 3rd chair as a junior. I now lead the Advanced Orchestra as 1st chair, performing ABRSM Level 5 to 7 repertoire across 7 school concerts. Violin is the one thing in my life that refused to be rushed; you cannot cram a clean vibrato the night before a concert. It taught me the patience that everything else I build now quietly depends on.

I co-founded Woodstock's AI Club because I was tired of watching classmates fear the tools I was already building with. Every week I lead more than 10 students through hands-on sessions on Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Lovable, and real prompt engineering, the kind of work where you break something, read the error, and fix it yourself. The goal was never to teach AI as magic. It was to make a room of people who treat it as an instrument, not an oracle.

As Editor in Chief I run the full production of our school yearbook: I have designed over 50 pages, overseen layout and editing across a team, and photographed content for the school's social media. A yearbook is a strange deadline, one book, one shot, no reprints, and hundreds of people expecting to find themselves in it done right. Leading it taught me that design is really decision-making under constraint, and that someone has to own the last call.

Over five years of varsity football I played goalkeeper and defender across more than 7 tournaments and 25 matches, contributing to over 18 team wins in regional competition. Both positions share one job: you are the last line, and your best games are the ones nobody notices because nothing got past you. That is a strange pride to learn young, being measured by the disasters you quietly prevent rather than the goals you loudly score.

As a varsity shooting guard I competed in more than 4 tournaments and 20 matches, helped the team to over 11 wins, and finished 1st at the THS Regional Tournament. Where football taught me to prevent, basketball taught me to take the shot; a shooting guard who hesitates is useless. Playing both trained two instincts most people only pick one of: the patience to defend, and the nerve to pull the trigger when the moment is mine.

I completed two hands-on engineering internships in India. At KGOC I worked through product development end to end, watching an idea move from concept to a finished, manufacturable object. At BAUM I learned CAD fundamentals and industrial design inside a real engineering environment, turning sketches into precise models. Classrooms teach you the equations; a shop floor teaches you the tolerances, the trade-offs, and the fact that a design is not real until someone can actually build it.

I held two senior intern roles at Woodstock at once. As Estates Head Intern I managed campus logistics and the unglamorous machinery that keeps a boarding school running. As Alumni Senior Intern I rebuilt bridges between graduates and current students, reconnecting people to a place they had left. One role was about maintaining a system, the other about maintaining a community. Both taught me that institutions run on the quiet work nobody applauds.

extracurriculars.organization: Outdoor Education, Woodstock School and Negi Wilderness Camp
extracurriculars.description: Through multi-day expeditions with Woodstock and Negi Wilderness Camp I earned certifications in Leave No Trace hiking, Wilderness First Aid, adult and child CPR, and Epi-Pen administration. The Himalayas do not care about your GPA. They teach a blunter syllabus: carry your own weight, leave nothing behind, and know exactly what to do in the ten minutes before help can arrive. Those are the skills I hope I never need and am very glad to have.

In Grade 10 I organized Service Learning Day 2024, coordinating 210 students across 20 groups for a day of inclusive activities and mural painting with underprivileged children. Logistics at that scale is its own quiet engineering: 210 people only move smoothly when someone has thought through the parts they never see. What stayed with me was not the murals we finished but how quickly the barrier between our students and the children dissolved once they were painting the same wall.

My independent STEM research runs on two tracks. My Math AA HL Extended Essay, 'To Punt Or To Play,' models 4th-down decisions in American football using a mixed-strategy Nash Equilibrium and win probability. My Physics HL IA investigates how a paper plane's wing surface area affects its flight time, my first real handshake with aerodynamics. One project is game theory, the other is fluid mechanics, and both come from the same instinct: take something I love watching, and ask exactly why it behaves the way it does.

extracurriculars.organization: Academic Honesty Council (AHC) and NHS, Woodstock School
extracurriculars.description: Beyond the titles, the Academic Honesty Council and National Honor Society are where I do the actual work of leadership. On the AHC I have sat through more than 30 hearings and delivered an INIA webinar to over 80 students; through NHS I have organized more than 20 service events. The common thread is unglamorous responsibility: showing up for the parts of a school that only work when someone chooses to care about fairness and service when nobody is checking.

honors.description: Out of a cohort of 85, I finished DP1 with the highest overall IB Diploma score in my year. It was not one exam; it was thirteen months of HL Physics, Math AA, and Computer Science stacked on three SL subjects, all held steady at once. I have never called it valedictorian, since the title is unofficial, but ranking first across that load is the result I am proudest to have earned quietly.

honors.issuer: International Journal of High School Research (IJHSR)
honors.description: At sixteen I published a full research paper, 'The Rise of Digital Trading: Accessibility Versus Risk of Financial Ruin,' in the International Journal of High School Research, an internationally peer-reviewed journal. It was not a class assignment; I chose the question, gathered the data across trading platforms, and argued it through to the end. Seeing my name in print taught me that research is less about being certain and more about being precise.

I am one of only two high schoolers ever selected as a Student Ambassador for the European Network for Academic Integrity, placed in a cohort otherwise made of PhD, Master's, and university candidates. I advise on integrity, referencing, and research ethics at an international level. Being the youngest voice in a room of doctoral researchers taught me to earn a seat by contributing, not by waiting to be old enough for it.

I serve on Woodstock's Academic Honesty Council, the student body that hears and rules on integrity cases at school, regional, and national levels. Across more than 30 hearings I learned that integrity is rarely about catching people; it is about building a culture where honesty is the easy choice. I also ran an INIA webinar for over 80 students, turning a rulebook into a conversation my peers could actually use.

Induction into the National Honor Society recognized four things at once: scholarship, service, leadership, and character. I did not treat it as a line on a page. As a member I organized more than 20 service events, because the honor only means something if it keeps producing work after the ceremony ends. The pin was the start of the obligation, not the reward for it.

I was chosen as Woodstock's school-wide Spanish Language Ambassador, one student out of roughly 250. The role meant representing the language and its culture across campus, supporting students learning it, and keeping Spanish alive beyond the classroom walls. For someone who grew up switching between Punjabi, Hindi, and English, being trusted to carry a fourth language felt less like an award and more like a natural extension of how I already live.

I was named to the Honor Roll as one of 15 students recognized for academic achievement across the school. It is not a single strong result; it is a full year of not letting the average slip while the IB load only climbs. Consistency is quieter than a prize, and harder to hold. That is exactly why this one means what it does to me.

I placed second school-wide in the E-Assessment, a timed evaluation of academic and analytical ability. Finishing near the very top under exam conditions proved something my coursework alone cannot: that I can think fast and accurately when the clock is the loudest thing in the room. Depth and speed are different skills. This is the one that says I have both.

whyAerospace.heading: Why Aerospace?
whyAerospace.subtitle: The honest answer.
paragraphs: I was three years old in a red toy Formula 1 car before I knew what a car really was, and I have been chasing the same feeling ever since. F1 taught me my first physics: that races are won and lost in how air bends around a machine, that a wing is just an upside-down promise, that milliseconds hide inside millimeters. That obsession with aerodynamics grew up alongside me, from taping wings onto paper planes to a Physics HL investigation on wing surface area and a Math HL derivation of the lift equation.

But aerodynamics only pulled me to the door. Propulsion is the reason I walked through it. The part that genuinely keeps me up is thrust: how you take stored energy and turn it into controlled, enormous force, how a column of plasma or a breath of burning air can move a body through a sky or past an atmosphere. Aerodynamics is how a machine survives the air. Propulsion is how it refuses to be held by it. That refusal is the engineering I want to spend my life on.

photos.alt: In a toy F1 car as a toddler

whySchool.defaultTemplate: I have long been drawn to {school} for the way it sits at the intersection of rigorous engineering and genuine intellectual ambition. Your programs in aerospace and technology match exactly where I want to push my work in AI, physics, and research. I am confident I can both learn from and contribute meaningfully to the {school} community.

schools.bocconi: Bocconi is the one school on my list where I get to chase the other half of me. Not the wings, the code. I have built five apps, from an AI finance advisor to an alumni network, co-founded my school's AI Club, and published data-driven research on digital trading, and Bocconi's BSc in Mathematical and Computing Sciences for Artificial Intelligence is the rare program that treats mathematics, computer science, and AI as one rigorous subject rather than three electives. Sitting in Milan, at a university built on economics and decisions, it would let me study the machinery of intelligence surrounded by people asking what it is actually for. I do not want to just use these tools. I want to understand what makes them work.
schools.georgia-tech: Georgia Tech runs the largest aerospace program in the country, and I care about one specific corner of it. The Ben T. Zinn Combustion Laboratory works across every kind of chemical propulsion, gas turbines, high-speed air-breathing engines, and chemical rockets, and next door the High-Power Electric Propulsion Lab holds the largest university vacuum facility in the nation for testing plasma thrusters. Chemical fire on one side, ionized gas on the other, thrust on both. That is the entire spectrum of the question I want to spend my life on, under one school's roof. Georgia Tech would not make me pick a lane in propulsion before I have even walked the whole road. It would just hand me the road.
schools.harvard:
Harvard is the one school on my list with no aerospace major, and I applied anyway, which forced me to be honest about what I actually want. What I want is the S.B. in Mechanical Engineering at SEAS, and the fluid mechanics underneath it: the Navier-Stokes equations, vorticity, lift and drag, the exact math I first met taping wings onto paper planes. The missing aero label does not scare me. It just means I get to build the path instead of following a sign.

And the building here is real. The Harvard Undergraduate Aerospace Collective launched the first student-built satellite in Harvard's history, a CubeSat that went from a grant proposal to Cape Canaveral, and its rocketry team is firing Mojave Sphinx, the Ivy League's first student-led liquid bi-propellant rocket. That is the maker culture I want to be inside.

There is a quieter reason too. I have spent five years translating between Ludhiana and Woodstock, and I think best where engineering sits beside everything else. Harvard would let me take Government and Economics next to my fluid dynamics, and treat that not as a distraction but as the whole point.
schools.hku-berkeley: I have spent five years living in two places at once, boarding at Woodstock in the Himalayas and going home to Ludhiana in Punjab, translating myself at every border. So a degree built out of two worlds does not intimidate me; it feels like home. The HKU and Berkeley dual degree puts my first two years in Hong Kong, at the heart of Asia, and my last two at Berkeley, the top public university in the world and now home to a new aerospace program. I would study engineering across two continents, two teaching cultures, and two ideas of what a problem even is. I already know how to be a person in more than one place. This is the version of that skill I would choose.
schools.nus: I have already sat in an NUS lecture hall. At the NUS Science Summer Camp I listened to Professor Sow Chorng Haur explain nanotechnology, and it was the first time I watched research feel less like a textbook and more like a live question. NUS Mechanical Engineering, with its aerospace track, sits at the center of Asia's fastest-moving research scene, close to the industry and the funding that turn ideas into hardware. Studying there would mean building in the region I am from, not away from it. I got a two-week taste of what NUS does to the way you think. I want the four-year version.
schools.princeton:
Most schools made me translate my aerospace dream into a nearby major. Princeton is the one that let me say the word out loud. In its combined Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering department I can point directly at the thing I care about most: propulsion. I emailed Professor Edgar Choueiri, whose Electric Propulsion and Plasma Dynamics Lab has been pushing plasma thrusters since before I was born, because his lab is where the question that keeps me up at night actually gets worked on: how do you turn energy into controlled, enormous force. A course like MAE 426, on rocket and air-breathing propulsion, is not a wishlist item for me; it is the syllabus I would build for myself if nobody were grading it.

But Princeton is not only a lab to me. It is a place that would let me keep both halves of who I am. I sit first chair in an orchestra and I want to design engines, and I have slowly realized those are not two lives but one. The physics that carries a rocket off a pad is the same physics that carries a note off a string. Princeton is where I would finally get to work in that overlap on purpose.
schools.purdue: If propulsion has a home, it is Purdue. This is where Maurice Zucrow taught America's first university course in rocket and jet propulsion and built its first academic Rocket Lab, and the Zucrow Laboratories are still the largest academic propulsion facility in the world, with real test cells firing real rocket and jet hardware. It is called the Cradle of Astronauts for a reason: Neil Armstrong learned aerospace here, and most of Purdue's astronauts came through this same school. For someone whose favorite part of aerospace is thrust, applying anywhere and skipping Purdue would feel dishonest. This is the place that decided propulsion was worth teaching first. I would like to learn it where it started.
schools.tu-delft: TU Delft holds the only aerospace faculty in the Netherlands and one of the largest in the world, and it is built for people who learn by testing. It runs subsonic, supersonic, and hypersonic wind tunnels reaching past Mach 11, flies its own Cessna as a flying classroom, and builds its own satellites in its own clean room. For someone who first fell for aerospace watching air bend around a Formula 1 car and then measured wing surface area against flight time in a Physics IA, a faculty this obsessed with the physical experiment is the obvious place to go deeper. I do not just want to derive the lift equation. I want to walk into the tunnel and watch it hold.
schools.tum: TUM keeps its aerospace department in Ottobrunn, minutes from Munich's aerospace cluster, where Airbus Defence and Space and the engine builder MTU sit within reach of the lecture hall. Its Chair of Turbomachinery and Flight Propulsion works on exactly the machinery I care about most, the turbines and engines that turn fuel into thrust. Germany's top-ranked aerospace program, planted next to the companies that actually build the hardware, means the gap between a lecture and a real engine is unusually small there. I like that. I do not want to study propulsion at a comfortable distance from industry. I want to study it close enough to hear the test stand.
schools.uc-berkeley: Berkeley just did something that suits me: it launched a full Aerospace Engineering major, built on top of one of the deepest fluid mechanics and combustion traditions in the country, at the top public university in the world. A new program at an old powerhouse is a rare combination, the ambition of something being built now with the rigor of a place that has taught these fundamentals for a century. My work keeps circling fluids and thrust, the lift equation, wing surface area, the physics of an engine, and Berkeley is where I could push those fundamentals as hard as they can be pushed. I like the idea of joining a program while it is still deciding what it will become.
schools.uc-davis: UC Davis offers a degree it actually calls Aerospace Science and Engineering, and it backs the name with real facilities, including an aeronautical wind tunnel and a department strong in aerodynamics, unsteady flows, and aeroacoustics. That experimental, air-first character is exactly where I started, taping wings onto paper planes and timing how long they stayed up. Davis pairs that hands-on aerodynamics with the reach of the UC research system, so the fundamentals I love come with the resources to chase them further. I am drawn to programs that still put you in front of moving air and ask you to explain it. Davis is one of them.
schools.uc-irvine: UC Irvine is quietly one of the best places in the country to study combustion, and combustion is just propulsion's beating heart. Its Combustion Laboratory is a serious research operation, and its aerospace track teaches propulsion directly, from gas turbines to ramjets, scramjets, and rockets, with current work reaching into detonation engines, one of the more exciting frontiers in how we make thrust. For someone whose favorite question in all of aerospace is how you turn stored energy into force, UCI puts that question at the center rather than the edge. I do not want propulsion as a single elective near the end. I want it as the reason I am there.
schools.uc-san-diego: UC San Diego runs its aerospace degree inside a Mechanical and Aerospace department that ranks among the very best in the country, first among public engineering schools for how often its research is cited. Its strengths sit right on my line: computational fluid dynamics, flow control, and hypersonics, the fast, hard end of the aerodynamics I first met watching Formula 1. Studying there would mean learning fluids and thrust from people whose work other researchers keep building on. I want to be somewhere the aerodynamics is not just taught but actively pushed forward. San Diego is one of the few places doing both at once.
schools.ucla: UCLA is where I would get to study the strangest, most exciting kind of thrust. Its Plasma and Space Propulsion Laboratory works on electric propulsion, moving spacecraft by accelerating ionized gas in electromagnetic fields, and the department teaches rocket propulsion directly. That is the frontier edge of the thing I love most: not fire and fuel, but plasma and fields quietly pushing a craft across space. Set inside one of the top Mechanical and Aerospace departments in the country, UCLA would let me chase propulsion past its familiar chemical form into what comes next. I am fascinated by thrust in every form it takes. UCLA studies the form most people have never seen.
schools.bath: Bath builds its aerospace degree the way I like to learn, foundations first, then specialization, with a full year working inside a real engineering company. You spend the early years on core mechanical engineering, the actual bedrock of flight, before narrowing into aerodynamics and propulsion, and Bath's tight industry links mean that narrowing happens next to people who build for a living. I trust programs that make you earn the specialism rather than handing it to you on day one. A year on an actual engineering floor, turning equations into tolerances, is exactly the kind of gap I want closed before I graduate. Bath closes it on purpose.
schools.bristol: Bristol sits at the historic center of British aerospace. Just up the road in Filton, the Bristol Aeroplane Company built its first aircraft in 1910 and the last Concorde ever flown now rests, and the same site still houses Airbus, Rolls-Royce, and GKN. The university grew up inside that ecosystem, home to the National Composites Centre and a course organized around the three things I keep returning to: aerodynamics, dynamics and control, and structures and materials. Studying aerospace minutes from where the wings of real aircraft are designed is a different kind of education. Bristol does not teach flight as history. It teaches it in the town that has been building it for over a century.
schools.uiuc: Illinois is where two halves of me overlap. Its Aerodynamics Research Laboratory runs wind tunnels on exactly the things I love, including motorsports aerodynamics, and the well-known UIUC airfoil and propeller databases came out of that same lab, the kind of data I have actually leaned on. Down the hall, the Electric Propulsion Laboratory fires arcjets and pulsed plasma thrusters and is developing new small-satellite propulsion concepts. Race-car airflow on one side, spacecraft thrusters on the other: my Formula 1 origin and my propulsion obsession sitting in one department. Illinois is a top aerospace program that happens to study both of the things that pulled me into this. That overlap is not a coincidence I want to waste.
schools.manchester: Manchester is where fluid mechanics grew a spine. Osborne Reynolds did his work here, and every time I write a Reynolds number in an aerodynamics problem I am using a piece of thinking that started in this university. For someone whose entire path runs through how fluids behave, from a paper-plane wing IA to the lift equation, studying at the place that helped define the field is more than symbolic. Manchester pairs that heritage with modern wind tunnels, deep industry links, and membership in the UK's aerospace research network. I like learning a subject where it was partly invented. It reminds you that the equations were once somebody's open question too.
schools.melbourne: Melbourne is built for someone with more than one obsession. Its model has you take a broad undergraduate degree first and then specialize through a Master of Engineering, so aerospace comes after a wider foundation rather than instead of one. For me, that is a feature, not a delay. I am a violinist who wants to design engines, a builder of AI apps who publishes research; I do my best thinking where subjects touch. A structure that lets me go wide before I go deep suits how my curiosity actually works. Melbourne would let me become an aerospace engineer without pretending I was only ever one thing.
schools.michigan: Michigan runs one of the oldest aerospace departments in the country and, more importantly to me, the Plasmadynamics and Electric Propulsion Laboratory, a world leader in the electric thrusters that will push the next generation of spacecraft. Its X3 thruster is being developed with NASA with an eye toward carrying humans to Mars. Add ten wind tunnels covering everything from micro air vehicles to above Mach 4, and Michigan gives me both ends of what I love, the air a machine flies through and the thrust that moves it. I am chasing propulsion specifically because of moments like a thruster built for Mars. Michigan is one of the few places actually building that moment.
schools.sheffield: Sheffield understands that an aircraft is not just designed, it is made. Its Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre, built in partnership with Boeing, is one reason the university ranks in the UK's top five for aeronautical and manufacturing engineering, and it means students learn aerospace with the manufacturing floor in view, not just the equation on the page. I have already felt that gap in my CAD and product-development internships, where a design is not real until someone can build it. Sheffield closes that gap by treating making as part of engineering, not an afterthought. I want to design things that can actually be built. Sheffield teaches you both halves.
schools.southampton: Southampton runs the largest specialist aeronautics degree in the UK and the R.J. Mitchell Wind Tunnel, named after the man who designed the Spitfire, the same tunnel Formula 1 teams have used to test their cars. That single fact ties together everything that pulled me into aerospace: the F1 aerodynamics I grew up on and the aircraft engineering I want to build a life in, tested in the same room. It is also the only Russell Group course that combines aeronautics and astronautics, air and space in one degree, with a vacuum chamber for spacecraft propulsion testing on site. For someone who came to aerospace through downforce and stayed for thrust, Southampton feels almost tailor-made.
